newsitem.title: UK: Smiths share price fall puzzles analysts.
newsitem.headline: Smiths share price fall puzzles analysts.

text.p: Shares in avionics to medical products group Smiths Industries Plc reversed early gains on Wednesday, falling 15 pence to 780-1/2 by 1300 GMT after half-year results had been digested.
The company said recent strength in sterling had affected British exports in its medical division but margins had improved and its substantial U.S. business "made satisfactory progress".

Analysts said they had been reassured about the medical business at a results briefing and looked forward to profits taking off in the aerospace division, which was enjoying the beginnings of an upturn in both civil and military aircraft production, particularly with its key U.S. customers Boeing and McDonnell Douglas.

"I am slightly at a loss to explain it (the share price fall)," said Nick Cunningham at brokers BZW. "It has to be said that this stock like all the other highly-rated stocks is subject to the odd wobble," he said.
"I think there was a bit of overreaction to the fact that Medical was flat," he said.

Several other analysts agreed. "I think the thing that has probably concerned people is that the Medical Systems business basically reported that turnover was down and profits were flat to slightly up," said one analyst with another broker, who declined to be named.

"Historically this has been a business which has shown very strong reported growth and although the company did a very good job of explaining the impact of foreign exchange, and I think just to see it in black and white as a business that didn't grow in the first half was just a bit of a shock for some people."
Smiths said the division, which specialises in single-use products and surgical equipment, were held back by the strength of sterling and sales dipped 3.7 million pounds to 142.2 million pounds.
But operating margins at the famously profitable division rose to 22.4 percent from 21.6 percent a year ago to leave operating profits up 300,000 pounds at 31.9 million pounds.
Chairman Sir Roger Hurn said profits at the division would probably have been about two million pounds higher had it not been for the effects of sterling on exports.

"It is a premium margin business," Hurn told Reuters earlier in an interview. "Our policy particularly over this period has been not to chase sales at the expense of margin but to make sure that we make quality sales and maintain margins," he said.
Hurn said the impact of sterling's strength on the group's overall results was limited because more than half of the company's manufacturing was based overseas.
He estimated that the overall impact was to reduce profits by about two million pounds in translation of foreign earnings and by a further two million due to the medical division's export business.
"I don't think it's a very big effect. We're less affected by this than some other UK-based companies," he said.

Meanwhile the company said an upturn in the aerospace industry helped boost its half-year profits by 15 percent and said it expected earnings to go on growing, despite a slowdown in growth in the medical products division.

Group profits for the six months to February 1 rose to 80.2 million pounds from 69.5 million pounds last year on sales up six percent at 495.3 million pounds. An exceptional gain on a property sale added a further 4.0 million pounds to the pre-tax result.
The dividend was raised 10 percent to 6.15 pence a share, in line with market forecasts, on post-exceptional earnings up 22 percent at 18.9 pence a share.

The company said it was now starting to enjoy the first fruits of recovery in output by aircraft manufacturers and the rationalisation of its Aerospace division during the lean years of recession now promised a further boost in profit margins as sales rise.

Operating profits at the division rose 5.7 million pounds to 22.9 million in the half year on sales up 12.7 million at 184.1 million pounds, an increase in operating margin of 2.4 points to 12.4 percent.

"If at the early stage of the (upturn in the aerospace business) cycle we can be improving margins like this then I would expect to see that improvement sustained," chairman Sir Roger Hurn told Reuters in an interview.
"At the peak of the last boom (in the aerospace industry cycle) in 1992 we were making between 15 and 16 percent margins. The fact is that this is the start of an upturn," he said.
BZW's analyst said he was contemplating an upgrade of his current year forecast to 196 million pounds for underlying pretax profits from 190 million and to 44.4 pence for earnings from 43.1 pence.
For the 1997/98 year he has pencilled in an upgrade in profits to 220 million pounds from 208 million currently.
"If one makes even very modest assumptions about operational gearing then all of our (analysts') forecasts are then far too low and aerospace profits should run away," said Cunningham.

Operating profits at the Industrial division, where products range from flexible tubing to domestic electrical timer switches, rose five million pounds to 26.6 million on sales up 20.1 million at 169 million pounds, with operating margins rising to a record 15.7 percent from 14.5 percent a year ago. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
